question.problem:
Consider the function $y = x^5 (\cos x)^x.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
y'(x) = x^4 (\cos x)^x \left( 5 + g(x) \right).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
question.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y = x^5 (\cos x)^x.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{5}{x}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y = x^5 (\cos x)^x {:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{5}{x}+\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{x}-\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(5+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = x \ln ( \cos  x ) - x^2 \tan x.
$$
